people.name: Hussein Samatar
body: In 2010, Minneapolis voters elected Hussein Samatar to the Board of Education. MPR News and MNopedia both describe him as the first Somali American in Minnesota, and most likely the country, to win elected public office. Samatar himself preferred the words "American of Somali descent." As he told a reporter that year, he remained part of the Somali diaspora, and he had made Minnesota his home.

Samatar was born in Kismayo, the youngest of five, and earned an economics degree at Somali National University in Mogadishu. By MNopedia's account he graduated in January 1991, four days before rebels overthrew the government. He fled to a refugee camp in Kenya and reached Minneapolis in 1994. He taught himself English using the computers and books at Franklin Library in East Phillips.

He became a business banker at Wells Fargo and earned an MBA from the University of St. Thomas. He then left banking to found the African Development Center, which offers immigrants and refugees financial education, loans, and training in business and homeownership. MPR News dates the founding to 2004; MNopedia dates it to 2002. The center says today that its clients face language, cultural and religious barriers, and it describes its loan pricing as a fixed interest rate or return on investment.

Mayor R.T. Rybak appointed him to the Minneapolis Library Board in the mid-2000s, and in 2008 he helped chair the committee that won a $60 million schools levy. On the school board he pressed for better results for students of color. He served until he died of complications from leukemia on August 25, 2013, at age 45. In 2018 Minneapolis opened Samatar Crossing, a bike and pedestrian path between Cedar-Riverside and downtown, named in his honor.
keyFacts: 1968: Born in Kismayo, Somalia, according to MNopedia's text.
1994: Settled in Minneapolis after time in a Kenyan refugee camp.
2002 or 2004: Founded the African Development Center (sources differ).
2008: Helped chair a successful $60 million Minneapolis schools levy.
2010: Elected to the Minneapolis Board of Education.
August 25, 2013: Died of complications from leukemia, age 45.
2018: Samatar Crossing opened in Minneapolis.
people.connectToWork: Does a benefit, loan or payment plan you handle assume something a person's faith may rule out? How would you find that out, and what alternatives could you offer?

people.name: Abdi Warsame
body: On election night in November 2013, supporters in Minneapolis's 6th Ward celebrated an upset. Abdi Warsame had defeated incumbent council member Robert Lilligren with about 63 to 64 percent of the first-choice vote. MPR News reported that he was the first person of Somali descent to hold municipal office in the United States.

The 6th Ward includes Cedar-Riverside. Warsame had directed the Riverside Plaza Tenants Association, and in 2012 he founded the Citizens Committee for Fair Redistricting, which helped redraw City Council ward boundaries, including Ward 6. After his win he said he hoped the election would transform the way Somalis see politics.

He took office in January 2014 and won re-election in 2017. In March 2020 he left the council to become executive director and CEO of the Minneapolis Public Housing Authority. Sahan Journal reported that the appointment made him the first Somali to lead a government agency in Minnesota.

As of October 2026 he leads the housing authority. In June 2026 the Minneapolis NAACP called for him to resign or be fired over conditions at the Heritage Park complex. The authority answered that it does not own, control or operate those units and that the NAACP had rushed to judgment. No report of how the dispute ended was found.
keyFacts: 2012: Founded the Citizens Committee for Fair Redistricting.
November 2013: Elected to the Minneapolis City Council, Ward 6.
2017: Re-elected.
March 2020: Became executive director and CEO of the Minneapolis Public Housing Authority.
June 2026: The Minneapolis NAACP called for his removal over Heritage Park; the housing authority disputed its account.
people.connectToWork: When ward lines, service areas or eligibility zones are drawn, who was in the room? How would the people living there find out, and how could they object?

people.name: Fartun Weli
body: Isuroon, on East Lake Street in Minneapolis, gives Somali women and girls a place to talk about their health. Its founder and CEO, Fartun Weli, has explained that the name is hard to translate in a few words. Mary's Pence gives the short form: a woman who cares for herself.

Weli founded Isuroon in 2010. By the account of the grant maker Mary's Pence, it grew from her own experience of struggling with cultural pressures around women's reproduction. In a 2019 profile she said, "There are things I'm not good at, but I am good at is busting down doors." She said her aim was that Somali women and girls not become dependent on the system.

In November 2015 Isuroon held its first "Safe Mothers, Safe Newborns" conference at the University of Minnesota's Humphrey School of Public Affairs. By 2019 the organization had bought its building on East Lake Street. Its teaching has covered female genital cutting, mental health, reproductive health, domestic and sexual violence, and finding a way through the health care system.

Isuroon has since grown well beyond health education. Its website now describes a halal food shelf started in 2016, therapy and mental health services, housing counseling, doula services, and refugee and youth programs. As of October 2026 Weli is its CEO. In April 2026 MPR News featured her in coverage of Somali Day at the State Capitol.
keyFacts: 2010: Founded Isuroon in Minneapolis.
November 12, 2015: Isuroon's first "Safe Mothers, Safe Newborns" conference.
2016: Isuroon's halal food shelf began.
April 2026: Featured in MPR News coverage of Somali Day at the Capitol.
people.connectToWork: If a person wants a woman provider or interpreter for a health conversation, what would it take to arrange that in your service, and how would they know they can ask?

people.name: Abdirahman Kahin
body: In May 2023, during National Small Business Week, the U.S. Small Business Administration named Abdirahman Kahin the National Small Business Person of the Year. He is the founder of Afro Deli & Grill.

Kahin came to the United States from Somalia in 1996. By Sahan Journal's account he attended community college and worked at a media company before opening his first location in Cedar-Riverside in 2010. He wanted to share the tastes of Africa and fill a gap in the Twin Cities food scene. In 2014 he launched Afro Deli & Grill as a fast-casual restaurant with a halal menu.

Sahan Journal reported in 2023 that the business had four Twin Cities locations plus grab-and-go food at Minneapolis–St. Paul International Airport. After his third application it joined the Minnesota State Fair as a new vendor that year. He told Sahan Journal that he wanted Afro Deli to become the first national African restaurant chain in the United States. As of October 2026 the company's website lists two restaurants, in downtown St. Paul and at Stadium Village in Minneapolis.

Somali-owned businesses are also part of the wider Minnesota economy. AP and MNopedia say Karmel Mall in south Minneapolis holds more than a hundred small businesses, the owner told Sahan Journal in June 2026 that it holds 650, and KALW/MPR says hundreds. AP reported in January 2026 that an immigration enforcement surge had left many of them empty.
keyFacts: 1996: Came to the United States from Somalia.
2010: First location opened in Cedar-Riverside, Minneapolis.
2014: Launched Afro Deli & Grill as a fast-casual restaurant.
2023: Named Minnesota, then national, Small Business Person of the Year; first year at the Minnesota State Fair.
October 2026: The company website lists two restaurants.
people.connectToWork: When your program serves food at a meal, event or care setting, who decides what is on the menu? How would you learn what each person can eat without guessing from their name or dress?

people.name: Ifrah Mansour
body: On a darkened stage, a seven-year-old girl tries to make sense of the war breaking out around her. Ifrah Mansour's one-woman show How to Have Fun in a Civil War tells this story with puppetry, poetry and video, and with oral stories drawn from community interviews.

St. Cloud State University describes Mansour as a Somali, refugee, Muslim multimedia artist living in Minnesota. She told MPR News that she wrote the play from her own experience as a young child fleeing Somalia around 1991 and 1992. KVSC, the St. Cloud State radio station, says the play mirrors her experience of spending her childhood in a refugee camp.

She performed it at the Children's Theatre Company in Minneapolis in October 2016, telling MPR News it was suitable for children ages 6 and up. She performed it at the Guthrie Theater from February 24 to March 11, 2018, and that April at St. Cloud State, through the Midnimo partnership.

Her installation Can I Touch It was part of the I Am Somali exhibition at the Minneapolis Institute of Art, which St. Cloud State calls her first national museum exhibit. Her later projects included a Flying Refugees installation at the Minnesota Landscape Arboretum and the play Finding Fatima with Twin Cities Public Television.
keyFacts: October 2016: How to Have Fun in a Civil War at the Children's Theatre Company.
February–March 2018: Performed the play at the Guthrie Theater.
2018: Can I Touch It on view in I Am Somali at the Minneapolis Institute of Art.
April 13, 2018: Performed the play at St. Cloud State University.
people.connectToWork: Your forms and interviews may ask people about war or flight. What other ways could someone tell you what they want you to know, and who decides how much they say?

people.name: Halima Aden
body: In November 2016, at the Miss Minnesota USA pageant, 19-year-old Halima Aden became, as news reports put it, the first Somali American to take part in the competition. She finished in the top 15. She told reporters that being there was not about winning, and that beauty is within.

Aden said she was born in a Kenyan refugee camp and left at six. In later interviews she calls herself "Halima from Kakuma." She grew up in St. Cloud and was a student at St. Cloud State University when she entered the pageant.

NPR later summed up what followed: the cover of Vogue and the swimsuit edition of Sports Illustrated, runways for Fenty Beauty and Yeezy, and a reputation as the first supermodel to wear a hijab. Right after signing her first big contract, she told the BBC, she asked her agency to connect her with UNICEF, and she became an ambassador. Asked by NPR whether that work lived up to her hopes, she said it did not.

In November 2020 Aden said she was leaving the fashion industry because her hijab was being styled out of existence. "I'm not a cover girl," she told NPR. She later said she had no regrets. Her decision is hers: she shows one person's choices about faith, work and visibility, and they speak for no one else.
keyFacts: Born in a Kenyan refugee camp; left at six and grew up in St. Cloud.
November 2016: First Somali American in Miss Minnesota USA; top 15.
Covers included Vogue and Allure; became a UNICEF ambassador.
November 2020: Left the fashion industry, citing her faith.
people.connectToWork: Two people may share a faith and make opposite choices about dress or work. What would you avoid assuming about a person because of what they wear?

people.name: Iman
body: Around 1973, photographer Peter Beard spotted a University of Nairobi student on a street in Nairobi. That chance meeting started the career of Iman Mohamed Abdulmajid, who became one of the best-known models in the world.

Iman was born in Mogadishu on July 25, 1955, before the civil war, when Somalia was a newly independent nation. She studied political science in Nairobi and worked as a translator to help pay her tuition. Beard's offer to pay her persuaded her to pose, and she asked for the $8,000 she owed the college. She moved to New York to model.

She became a favorite of leading designers; Yves Saint Laurent devoted a collection to her, called "The African Queen." She retired from modeling in 1989. She married musician David Bowie in 1992, and they stayed married until his death in 2016. In 1994 she launched IMAN Cosmetics, a line created for women of color. Carnegie Corporation of New York named her a Great Immigrant in 2006.

In 1992, during famine and war, she convinced the BBC to let her take a film crew to Somalia, producing the documentary Somalia Diary. In 2019 she became the first Global Advocate for the humanitarian organization CARE. "I am the face of a refugee," The Root quoted in its headline.
keyFacts: July 25, 1955: Born in Mogadishu, Somalia.
About 1973: Discovered in Nairobi by photographer Peter Beard.
1989: Retired from modeling.
1992: Married David Bowie; made the BBC's Somalia Diary.
1994: Launched IMAN Cosmetics.
2019: Named CARE's first Global Advocate.
people.connectToWork: Before the war in Somalia, people worked, studied and built careers there. What does your process ask about the life and skills a person had before they came here?

people.name: Abdi Abdirahman
body: In February 2020, in Atlanta, a 43-year-old runner finished third at the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials in 2:10:03. That made Abdi Abdirahman a five-time Olympian. Four years earlier, at 39, he had placed third at the New York City Marathon, which USATF says made him the oldest man on that podium. Runners call him "the Black Cactus."

Abdirahman was born in Somalia on January 1, 1977, and moved to Arizona at age 12. He settled in Tucson and graduated from Tucson High School in 1995. He ran at Pima Community College and then the University of Arizona. He became a U.S. citizen on January 28, 2000, and that same year made his first U.S. Olympic team.
His Olympic record covers two decades. He ran the 10,000 meters at the 2000, 2004 and 2008 Games and the marathon in London in 2012 and at the Tokyo Games, held in 2021.
In 2021 he published a memoir, Abdi's World: The Black Cactus on Life, Running, and Fun. In April 2024 he was inducted into the Arizona Sports Hall of Fame.
keyFacts: January 1, 1977: Born in Somalia; moved to Arizona at age 12.
1995: Graduated from Tucson High School; later Pima Community College and the University of Arizona.
January 28, 2000: Became a U.S. citizen; first Olympics that year.
2016: Third at the New York City Marathon.
2020: Third at the U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials, at 43.
2024: Inducted into the Arizona Sports Hall of Fame.

people.name: Abdi Nor Iftin
body: In a story told on the public radio program This American Life, a young man in Kenya, hiding from police sweeps, won the U.S. Diversity Visa Lottery, in which about 8 million people compete each year for roughly 50,000 visas. Listeners around the country heard Abdi Nor Iftin's story before he ever reached the United States.

Iftin grew up in Mogadishu during the civil war. He fell in love with American movies and music, which earned him the nickname "Abdi American." He later fled to Kenya, where the Bangor Daily News reports he could not get a job with his refugee documents.

Iftin landed in Boston on August 11, 2014, and went on to Maine. He worked as a translator for Catholic Charities, going to hospitals and courts with Somali refugees. In 2018 Knopf published his memoir, Call Me American. He became a U.S. citizen in January 2020, and in 2022 Husson University described him as a Yarmouth, Maine, resident.
His story is a reminder that people come to the United States by different legal paths, including refugee resettlement, family reunification, asylum and the diversity visa.
keyFacts: Grew up in Mogadishu during the civil war; known as "Abdi American."
Won the U.S. Diversity Visa Lottery while living in Kenya.
August 2014: Arrived in the United States and settled in Maine.
2018: Published Call Me American (Knopf).
January 2020: Became a U.S. citizen.
people.connectToWork: Does your process assume how a person came to the United States? Which of your rules change with immigration status, and how would you ask only what you need to know?

people.name: Nuruddin Farah
body: In 1998, the University of Oklahoma's journal World Literature Today awarded its Neustadt International Prize for Literature to a Somali novelist, Nuruddin Farah. Kenyan writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o wrote that Farah "questions all the oppressive stabilities" and called him an important voice in postcolonial modernism.

Farah was born on November 24, 1945, in Baidoa, in what is now Somalia, and he writes in English. In the United States he has taught as Distinguished Professor of Literature at Bard College in New York.

He has written a series of novels called Variations on the Theme of an African Dictatorship: Sweet and Sour Milk, Sardines and Close Sesame. His Blood in the Sun trilogy is made up of Maps, Gifts and Secrets. His other novels include From a Crooked Rib, Links, Knots and Crossbones.

In 1991 he received Sweden's Tucholsky literary award, given to writers living in exile. In a 2020 interview shared by Bard he said, "I roamed the world, made the world my small village." By AALBC's account he lives in Cape Town, South Africa, with his family.
keyFacts: November 24, 1945: Born in Baidoa, Somalia.
1991: Received the Swedish Tucholsky literary award.
1998: Neustadt International Prize for Literature laureate.
Distinguished Professor of Literature at Bard College (2020 listing).
Lives in Cape Town, South Africa, according to AALBC.
people.connectToWork: What could your team read or listen to, written by people from the places your clients come from, before deciding what they need? Who would you ask for suggestions?

people.name: Said Salah Ahmed
body: In 2005 the McKnight Foundation gave its Virginia McKnight Binger Award in Human Service to Said Salah Ahmed, a Minneapolis teacher. He was by then a poet, a playwright and a lifelong educator on two continents.

By his own account, he was born in the northeast of Somalia, where as a child he herded goats and sheep and sailed with his father. He enrolled in school at six, began writing poetry at eleven, and traveled 120 miles by camel caravan to reach middle school. In eighth grade an assistant principal caught him teaching younger students in an empty classroom. He studied biology at the College of Education from 1968, then led a high school and later a teacher training school in Mogadishu.

He co-wrote one of Somalia's famous plays. When a second play led to a co-writer's jailing, he says, the group was censored and harassed. In 1979 Somalia awarded him a bronze medal for his educational, cultural and artistic work, and his song "Midwife" was voted one of the top four in a United Nations International Year of the Child song contest.

When civil war began he fled with his family. He says he founded what was then the largest school in a refugee camp, at Utanga in Kenya, and wrote and directed a 17-week BBC radio play on peace and reconciliation. In Minneapolis he became a bilingual teacher at Sanford Middle School, using a book he wrote, and taught Somali at the University of Minnesota. In 2017 the Minnesota Daily reported that he led monthly school presentations for the Somali Museum.
keyFacts: Born in northeastern Somalia.
1968: Began studies at Somalia's College of Education.
1979: Received Somalia's bronze medal for educational, cultural and artistic work.
Founded a school in Kenya's Utanga refugee camp after fleeing the war.
Taught at Sanford Middle School in Minneapolis and taught Somali at the University of Minnesota.
2005: Virginia McKnight Binger Award in Human Service.
people.connectToWork: When you meet an older adult who is new to English, what do you know about the work they did before? How might asking change what you offer them?

people.name: Hassan Mead
body: In August 2016, in the first round of the Olympic 5,000 meters in Rio de Janeiro, Minneapolis runner Hassan Mead collided with other runners and fell. His appeal to the International Olympic Committee was denied. That night, however, a jury of appeal reviewed new video evidence from Team USA and let him advance. He finished 11th in the final, in 13:09.81.

Mead's family moved to Minnesota from Somalia in 2000. He went to Minneapolis South High School, and in his one cross country season he went undefeated in Minnesota, won the Class AA state title and the Foot Locker Midwest Regional, and placed fourth at Foot Locker Nationals.

At the University of Minnesota, Mead became an eight-time All-American. He won three Big Ten indoor titles and four outdoor titles, and he was named the 2009 Big Ten Track Athlete of the Year. He graduated in 2012, and by MileSplit's account he holds school records in the indoor 5,000 meters and the outdoor 5,000 and 10,000 meters.
In 2016 he finished second in the 5,000 meters at the U.S. Olympic Trials and earned a place on the U.S. team.
keyFacts: 2000: Family moved to Minnesota from Somalia.
Won the Minnesota Class AA state cross country title for Minneapolis South High School.
2009: Big Ten Track Athlete of the Year; eight-time All-American.
2012: Graduated from the University of Minnesota.
2016: Second in the 5,000 m at the U.S. Olympic Trials.
August 2016: Reinstated to the Rio Olympic final after a fall; finished 11th.

people.name: Ladan Osman
body: In 2020, Ladan Osman's poetry collection Exiles of Eden won the Hurston/Wright Legacy Award. Coffee House Press had published it in 2019 in Minneapolis. In 2021 she received a Whiting Award in poetry.

Osman was born in Somalia and raised in Columbus, Ohio. She earned an MFA at the Michener Center for Writers at the University of Texas at Austin. She has received fellowships from the Lannan Foundation, Cave Canem, the Michener Center and the Fine Arts Work Center.

Her first collection, The Kitchen-Dweller's Testimony, was published by the University of Nebraska Press in 2015 after winning the Sillerman First Book Prize for African Poets. Her publisher describes Exiles of Eden as steeped in Somali narrative tradition and as giving voice to displaced people over several generations.

Osman also works in film. She was the writer of Sun of the Soil, a short documentary on the Malian emperor Mansa Musa, selected for the Cannes International PanAfrican Film Festival and the New York African Film Festival. She co-directed the short film Sam Underground, and The Ascendants was her directorial debut. She lives in New York.
keyFacts: Born in Somalia; raised in Columbus, Ohio; MFA, Michener Center for Writers.
2015: The Kitchen-Dweller's Testimony (University of Nebraska Press).
2019: Exiles of Eden (Coffee House Press, Minneapolis).
2020: Hurston/Wright Legacy Award.
2021: Whiting Award in poetry.
people.connectToWork: Whose words are in the stories your team tells about people who were displaced? How could you make room for what they have already said about themselves?

people.name: Idil Abdull
body: In October 2010 Idil Abdull, a Somali mother of a child with autism, spoke during public comment at the federal Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee. "If you want to know the answer to autism, come and study us," she said. The committee later credited her testimony with sparking a rapid federal response to investigate autism rates in Somali families in Minnesota.

Abdull lives in Burnsville and co-founded the Somali American Autism Foundation. In 2012, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius named her to that same federal committee. MPR News reported that she hoped to represent communities facing language, cultural or economic barriers in health care, and that she planned regular appearances in Somali media to update parents.

Abdull told the Minnesota Daily that she had never heard the word autism before her son was diagnosed at about two and a half, and that she now "eats, drinks and breathes autism." She also served on a Minnesota autism task force. The University of Minnesota's 2013 prevalence project, described on this page, began because Somali parents raised concerns. Her current role could not be established.
keyFacts: Lives in Burnsville, Minnesota; parent of an autistic son.
Co-founder of the Somali American Autism Foundation.
October 2010: Testified to the federal Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee.
2012: Appointed to that committee.
people.connectToWork: If families are raising a concern your system has not measured, how would you hear it, and what would you do before the data exists?

people.name: Mahdi Warsama
body: Mahdi Warsama is chief executive of the Somali Parents Autism Network and the parent of a child with autism. The University of Minnesota's Institute on Community Integration describes him as a strong advocate for children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorders, and he serves on its Community Advisory Council.

That places a parent-run network and a university disability research center in the same room. A 2014 Minnesota Department of Health report recommended building on parent leadership of this kind, and it called parents' willingness to support each other a potential untapped resource.
keyFacts: CEO of the Somali Parents Autism Network.
Parent of a child with autism.
Member of the Institute on Community Integration's Community Advisory Council.

institutions.name: Somali Museum of Minnesota
body: It began with one person's collecting. In 2009 Osman Ali, a Minneapolis café owner, began gathering artifacts of Somalia's traditional nomadic life and, by MNopedia's account, showing them in the basement of his restaurant, Sanaag Coffee. He traveled between Somalia and Minnesota and gave presentations at schools and community centers.

The museum says it was founded in 2011 and opened its public gallery in 2013; MNopedia dates the founding itself to 2013. It describes itself as North America's only Somali-focused museum. Its collection has grown from more than 700 artifacts in 2017 to more than 1,500 by its own count today, on display at 2925 Chicago Avenue.

The museum runs a dance program, weaving classes, monthly gallery sessions and group tours. In 2017 a bill sponsored by a then-state representative sought $200,000 in state money for program space. It is marking its 13th anniversary in 2026.
keyFacts: 2009: Osman Ali began collecting Somali artifacts.
2011: Founded, by the museum's account. 2013: Public gallery opened.
More than 1,500 artifacts, by its own count.
Open Thursday to Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., as of October 2026.
institutions.connectToWork: What could your team learn from a visit or a group tour here, and how would you pay for the staff time and expertise you are asking for?

institutions.name: Sahan Journal
body: In 2019, Mukhtar Ibrahim, a Somali-born journalist and former Star Tribune reporter, set out to build a newsroom devoted to Minnesota's immigrant and refugee communities. He named it Sahan, a Somali word meaning "pioneer."

Ibrahim came to the United States from Somalia in 2005 and has spent most of his life in Minnesota. He earned a journalism degree at the University of Minnesota and became MPR's first Somali American reporter. He later earned a graduate degree at Columbia University. In his coverage of the 2016 federal trials of Twin Cities men accused of trying to aid the Islamic State, courthouse security briefly barred him from the courtroom while admitting white reporters.

Ibrahim first started Sahan Journal in 2013 as a side project. In 2019, as a full-time MPR employee, he began relaunching it as a nonprofit newsroom covering all of Minnesota's immigrant communities. He said he wanted it to be "a one-stop shop for all things immigrant in Minnesota."

Ibrahim stepped down as CEO and publisher in October 2024. The newsroom continues, and it describes itself as dedicated to reporting for Minnesota's immigrants and communities of color. In 2026 Ibrahim founded a separate outlet, The Somali Brief, listed on this page.
keyFacts: 2013: Mukhtar Ibrahim launched Sahan Journal as a side project.
2019: Relaunched as a nonprofit newsroom, with support from MPR News.
"Sahan" means "pioneer" in Somali.
October 2024: Ibrahim stepped down as CEO and publisher.
institutions.connectToWork: Which news outlets do the people you serve actually read or hear? How would you find out before planning outreach?

institutions.name: Riverside Plaza
body: Riverside Plaza is a housing complex of towers and lower apartment blocks in the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood of Minneapolis. The National Park Service says about 4,400 people live there, most of them of East African descent, and calls it the largest affordable housing development in the Midwest.

Modernist architect Ralph Rapson designed it in the early 1970s, working with Lawrence Halprin; it was built as Cedar Square West under a federal program called New Towns In Town. By the Park Service's account, Rapson based the design on European urban housing that aimed to bring together residents of different cultures and incomes. What stands today is only the first of ten planned stages.

In December 2010 Riverside Plaza was individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places, despite local opposition to designating modern architecture. Sources give different counts of its buildings and units, so none is offered here.
keyFacts: Early 1970s: Designed by Ralph Rapson with Lawrence Halprin.
About 4,400 residents, most of East African descent, according to the National Park Service.
December 2010: Listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

institutions.name: Somali Parents Autism Network
body: By its own account, the Somali Parents Autism Network was founded in 2014 by a group of Somali American immigrant parents of children diagnosed with autism. Its stated mission is to educate and inform Somali families of children with autism in Minnesota through outreach and collaboration, connecting them with services, with the aims of early intervention and caregiver empowerment.

In fiscal year 2020 it received a $5,000 Arts and Cultural Heritage Fund microgrant through the Minnesota Humanities Center for family poetry, conversations on the history of disability, meetings on stigma with school staff, and parent peer support nights. In 2023 it joined CAIR-Minnesota and legislators at the State Capitol to press for autism safety measures after two children drowned. Parents there also described months-long waits for state services.
keyFacts: 2014: Founded by Somali American parents, by its own account.
CEO: Mahdi Warsama.
Work includes system navigation, parent-to-parent support and an awareness campaign.
institutions.connectToWork: Would you offer this network to a family as a peer connection? How would you make clear that it is their choice, and that it does not replace your agency's own duty to them?

institutions.name: Institute on Community Integration, University of Minnesota
body: The Institute on Community Integration is a University of Minnesota disability research center that began in 1985 with fewer than 20 staff. It published the 2013 Minneapolis Somali Autism Spectrum Disorder Prevalence Project community report, whose authors included Anab A. Gulaid, and it released a family fact sheet in English and Somali.

The National Institutes of Health lists the project's funders as the CDC, the NIH and Autism Speaks, through a competitive award made via the Association of University Centers on Disabilities. The institute also has a Community Advisory Council that includes parent leaders.
keyFacts: 1985: Began, with fewer than 20 staff.
Prevalence project funded by the CDC, NIH and Autism Speaks.
December 2013: Published the community report.
Family fact sheet available in English and Somali.

disability.intro: This background is intended to help you prepare questions. It does not describe any individual or family. Somali here refers to people who identify with Somalia or its diaspora, and who differ in generation, region, education, faith practices, and routes to Minnesota. Somali Bantu families may speak Maay Maay rather than standard Somali. Nearly all Minnesota research identified is about autism in children. No Minnesota study on physical, sensory, psychiatric, or adult disability among Somali Minnesotans was found, and none on Deaf or DeafBlind Somali Minnesotans. The two main reports cited are more than ten years old.
questions: What words does your family use to describe your child's needs, or your own?
What have you been told about why this happens, and what do you think?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Do you agree with it, and has it helped or got in the way?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who in your family should be part of these decisions or meetings? Is there anyone you would rather not include?
Are there people or places, such as a mosque, a parent group or relatives, that help you? Would you like us to work alongside them?
Have you had trouble getting a diagnosis or services before? What happened?
How do you want to get information: in writing, by phone, in person, through Somali-language radio or social media?
Would you like an interpreter? Is there anyone you would not want interpreting, such as someone you know, and do you prefer a woman or a man?
Would you like to meet other parents or people who have been through this, or would you rather not?

context.heading: How often autism has been identified
body: The University of Minnesota reviewed the clinical and educational records of more than 5,000 Minneapolis children aged 7 to 9 in 2010. MPR News reported that 1 in 32 Somali children were identified with autism, against 1 in 36 white children, a gap the researchers did not consider significant. The rates were 1 in 62 for non-Somali Black children and 1 in 80 for Hispanic children. All the Somali children identified also had an intellectual disability as measured by lower IQ scores. The lead researcher said the study was not designed to explain why.

Later monitoring in Hennepin and Ramsey counties, funded through the CDC, found for 2018 that 1 in 29 Somali 8-year-olds had autism, against 1 in 36 for 8-year-olds overall, and 1 in 21 Somali 4-year-olds, against 1 in 44 overall. Sahan Journal reported in 2024 that 1 in 16 Somali preschool children were diagnosed in 2020. The project's lead investigator told Sahan Journal in 2022 that the gap at age 4 may partly reflect earlier identification, and that more research is needed. These are counts of identified children in two counties. They say nothing about any one child or about cause.

sources.label: MPR News, "Study: Mpls. Somali, white children equally susceptible to autism" (2013)
Institute on Community Integration, Community Report 2013
Sahan Journal, "'Slow-minded' becomes 'unique mind'" (2022)
Sahan Journal, Maangaar Summit (held Sept. 2, 2024; article published Sept. 9, 2024)

context.heading: Words, and who is changing them
body: A 2014 Minnesota Department of Health report said the word autism did not exist in Somali, and that families might first hear it in a U.S. clinic or school. Parents in Minnesota have since worked on that themselves. Sahan Journal reported in 2022 that a group of parents, medical professionals and people with autism, meeting over Zoom and Clubhouse, settled on two terms: maangaar, unique mind, and maangooni, separate mind.

The same story lists older terms that advocates want to leave behind, including maangaab, slow-minded; qof jiran, sick person; and qof waalan, crazy person. Knowing them can help you hear what a person may fear, and help you brief an interpreter. Do not assume everyone knows or prefers the new terms. Ask, and use the words the person uses. No published work on Somali terms for other disabilities was found.

sources.label: Sahan Journal, "'Slow-minded' becomes 'unique mind'" (2022)
Minnesota Department of Health, Report to the Legislature (2014)

context.heading: What parents said about understanding and delay
body: The Department of Health study drew on 33 key informants and 70 parents, 38 of them Somali, compared with Hmong and Latino families. Among those 38 Somali parents, the most common accounts of autism were, in order: vaccines, unclear what it is, a mental problem or illness, spiritual causes, and a medical condition. About a quarter of informants said it was hard or impossible to generalize. The study did not report results by generation, region or education.

Parents usually noticed something first, and many sought help early. The report traced delays to individual knowledge and stigma, to providers through misdiagnosis, discrimination and language barriers, and to systems through waitlists and insurance. It found parents were "not passive." Check these system explanations first. Refer medical questions, including those about vaccines, to clinicians.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, Report to the Legislature (2014)

context.heading: Family, faith and support
body: In the same parent sample, Somali families averaged more than four children, about 19 percent were single-parent households, and fathers took part more often than in the Hmong or Latino groups. The report noted that immigrant families may be isolated from relatives who would otherwise help, and listed cultural ties, social connection and religious faith as strengths. It included four spiritual leaders or healers among its informants.

A 2020 Augsburg University nursing project with five Somali parents in Minneapolis found the themes of unfamiliarity with autism, fear of stigma, barriers to services, and acceptance, support and strong faith. Five parents is a small group. No source was found describing specific religious practices used for disability in Minnesota, or the role of clan or elders in these decisions, so ask rather than assume.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, Report to the Legislature (2014)
Safiya Ahmed, "Increasing Autism Awareness in the Somali Community," Augsburg University (2020)

context.heading: What families asked for, and working with interpreters
body: Somali parents in the 2014 report asked for autism education that fits their language, family support, culturally sensitive services, a community center and more funding for community autism groups. The report also recommended parent-leaders modeled on community health workers, respite care, and county specialists who share a family's language.

Use a trained Somali medical or community interpreter, not a child or relative. Plan extra time for terms such as autism, developmental delay and intellectual disability, and check understanding by asking the person to say it back. Give short written summaries in English and Somali where they exist.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, Report to the Legislature (2014)

context.heading: Disabled Somali leaders and who is missing
body: Parents have led most of the public work described here, including Idil Abdull and Mahdi Warsama, profiled on this page, and Anisa Hagi-Mohamed, who organized the 2024 Maangaar Summit in Bloomington. People with autism took part in the terminology work. At that summit Mahad Dahir, the son of Somali immigrants, who was diagnosed with autism at 2 and did not speak until he was 4, told Sahan Journal, "We need to tell our stories." He became student body president at Highline College in Washington state in 2022.
No Minnesota organization led by Somali disabled people was found. Do not treat any one person or group as speaking for everyone, and do not take a parent's account as the disabled person's own.

communityRoutes.name: Somali Parents Autism Network
communityRoutes.purpose: Peer support, system navigation and help with diagnosis and special education for Somali families of children with autism. A family's own choice, never a replacement for your agency's duties.

communityRoutes.name: Somali Community Resettlement Services
communityRoutes.purpose: Its United Way 211 listing describes work with the Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities on leadership training for people with disabilities in the Somali and Latino communities.

organizations.intro: These are starting points for learning, and the list is not complete. Listing here says nothing about who a person trusts, and no group speaks for everyone. The groups below include agencies, mosques, women's organizations, students and media, in Minneapolis, the suburbs, St. Cloud, Rochester and Faribault. AP reported in January 2026 that an immigration enforcement surge had emptied many Somali businesses. Before reading a missed contact as a lack of interest, ask what may have changed for that person.

sources.label: MPR News, Minnesota journalists launch The Somali Brief (Sept. 30, 2026)
Associated Press, Somali businesses during the Minneapolis enforcement surge (Jan. 18, 2026)
MNopedia (MNHS), "Confederation of Somali Community in Minnesota"

entries.name: Confederation of Somali Community in Minnesota
entries.purpose: Founded in 1994; MNopedia calls it one of the oldest Somali-run nonprofits in the state. Offers newcomer help with translation, housing and immigration, youth and education programs, job readiness, health and wellness, civic engagement, and an in-person support hub for Uber drivers. Business resource fairs were posted for fall 2026.

entries.name: Dar Al-Hijrah Mosque
entries.purpose: Opened in 1998 as the Riverside Islamic Center, described by Augsburg University as the oldest Somali mosque in Minnesota. Community members raised $400,000 to buy the building in 2006. It closed after water damage from a fire next door on January 1, 2014, which killed three people who lived above a neighboring store. The mosque was closed for more than a year and opened again in spring 2015. In April 2020 it began a public call to prayer during Ramadan, reported as believed to be the first in a major U.S. city.
entries.linkLabel: Augsburg University history of the mosque

entries.name: Abubakar As-Saddique Islamic Center
entries.purpose: One of the largest mosques in Minnesota, and by its imam's account a community center for the area, with classes and youth activities. It is connected to a school, Aim Academy of Science and Technology. Non-Muslim neighbors visit during Ramadan. In December 2024 a threat cancelled most weekend programs; police judged it not credible.

entries.name: Dar Al-Farooq Center
entries.purpose: Says it provides resources and services for Muslims and neighbors in Minnesota, with partners including VEAP and Sakan Community Resources, and that it advocates through the Muslim Coalition of ISAIAH. The center was bombed in August 2017. Three people from Clarence, Illinois, were arrested in 2018, and the case ended in federal convictions.
entries.linkLabel: FOX 9 coverage of the bombing case (2018)

entries.name: Somali Community Resettlement Services
entries.purpose: A nonprofit since 2000 that helps new arrivals with paperwork and U.S. systems. Its 211 listing also describes job help, ESL classes in Faribault, trauma counseling through a partner, programs for elders and youth, and suicide prevention planning with the Minnesota Department of Health. It also serves other East Africans and Latino residents. Its own site says it previously had offices in Rochester and Faribault; it does not say they remain open.

entries.name: Somali American Social Service Association
entries.purpose: Founded in 2012 to assist underserved immigrant communities in Olmsted County. It holds information sessions on health care, immigration, business and education. Omar Nur was founder and executive director in February 2025, according to KTTC. KTTC spells the name Somali America Social Services Association; Sahan Journal uses Somali American Social Service Association.

entries.name: African Development Center
entries.location: Minneapolis, 1931 South 5th Street; also St. Cloud, Rochester and Willmar
entries.purpose: Founded by Hussein Samatar, profiled on this page. Offers credit help, business planning and loans, and homebuyer education and counseling for African immigrants and others, in several languages. Its loan terms list a fixed interest rate or return on investment.

entries.name: Isuroon
entries.purpose: A Somali women-led organization founded in 2010 by Fartun Weli, profiled on this page. Its site lists a halal food shelf, therapy and mental health services, housing counseling, doula services, support for survivors of violence, youth programs, refugee support and a 24-hour crisis line.

entries.name: Ayada Leads
entries.purpose: Formerly known as the Women Organizing Women Network. Has worked since 2016 to help Somali and East African women become engaged citizens and community leaders, using its own Dumar Leadership Model. Mary's Pence lists it as a grantee.

entries.name: Karmel Mall
entries.location: South Minneapolis, near West Lake Street
entries.purpose: A commercial complex, not a nonprofit. AP describes more than a hundred small businesses (MNopedia agrees; the owner told Sahan Journal 650 in June 2026, and KALW/MPR says hundreds), from clothing and food to insurance and accounting, plus housing, a mosque and Quran classes. A second site is also listed at 200 W. Lake St. Many stores were shuttered during the January 2026 enforcement surge.

entries.name: CAIR-Minnesota
aliases: Council on American-Islamic Relations, Minnesota Chapter
entries.purpose: A Muslim civil rights organization, not specific to Somali Minnesotans. Works on Islamophobia, civil rights and community advocacy. Joined the Somali Parents Autism Network on autism safety advocacy at the Capitol.

entries.name: Muslim American Society Minnesota
entries.location: Several masjids, including Blaine, Rosemount and Coon Rapids
entries.purpose: A multi-ethnic Muslim organization that says it operates seven masjids in Minnesota. It offers religious and youth programs, social services and emergency help, a food shelf, and the annual Minnesota Muslim Convention.

entries.name: Somali Student Association, University of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Marked 28 years in 2026. Its Somali Night at Northrop was held on April 3, 2026. A separate University of Minnesota chapter of the Somali American Medical Association serves medical students.

entries.name: WellShare International
entries.purpose: Not Somali-led. Calls itself the pioneer of the community health worker model in Minnesota and serves 16 counties. As Minnesota International Health Volunteers, it began the Center for Somali Health in south Minneapolis.

entries.name: Somali Bilingual Book Project
entries.type: Completed literacy project, Minnesota Humanities Center
entries.purpose: A completed project. In 2007 it published four traditional Somali tales as children's books in Somali and English. Books For Africa later reprinted them, and in 2020 the Humanities Center followed with Crossroads, an anthology by 31 young Somali American writers.

entries.name: The Somali Brief
entries.purpose: Launched in September 2026 by Sahan Journal founder Mukhtar Ibrahim, with former WCCO reporter Ubah Ali as lead reporter. It covers Somali American life and says it challenges false claims. A for-profit company with a nonprofit fiscal sponsor.

entries.name: Somali TV of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Somali-language talk shows and news. Twin Cities Business named it in September 2026 as the first media partner of The Somali Brief.

entries.name: KALY-LP 101.7 FM
entries.purpose: Somali-language station with about a 10-mile range, also streaming online. It says it aims to celebrate, educate and inform Somali and East African immigrants. Its own site estimates about 40,000 Somali speakers in that range.

entries.name: KZYS-LP 105.1 FM
entries.purpose: St. Cloud's only Somali-language radio station as of a February 2024 profile, which estimates 7,000 to 10,000 listeners. Grew out of a 2013 web stream with KVSC at St. Cloud State. Carried COVID-19 information during the pandemic.

entries.name: Somali Link Radio
entries.purpose: An English-language show on the Somali community, begun in January 2017 and hosted by Abdirizak Bihi. Station playlists are logged on Tuesdays at 6 p.m. through at least March 2025.

entries.name: MPR News Somali
entries.purpose: Launched in February 2018, combining BBC World Service content with translated MPR News reports. It no longer appears to run as a separate service: mprnews.org/somali now sends readers to BBC Somali.

entries.name: City of Minneapolis cultural media (Somali)
entries.purpose: City information in Somali, including the program Magaaladayda Minneapolis, produced with Moon Media.

entries.name: Council on American-Islamic Relations
entries.purpose: National Muslim civil rights organization, with chapters including CAIR-Minnesota.

entries.name: Muslim American Society
entries.purpose: Says it is an Islamic charitable, religious, social, cultural and educational nonprofit, established in 1993. Its Minnesota affiliate is listed on this page.

entries.name: Somali Bantu Association of America
entries.purpose: Serves refugee families with ESL, employment help and community health workers, in languages including Somali and Maay Maay. Useful background for Somali Bantu families, who may not speak standard Somali. No current Somali Bantu organization in Minnesota was found.

entries.name: Somali Family Service of San Diego
entries.purpose: Established in 2000. Provides programs in children and youth, health, economic development and immigration, with translation and interpretation. Its site says it serves refugee and immigrant communities in California and Minnesota.

entries.name: Somali American Council of Oregon
entries.purpose: Founded in 2010. Works to strengthen links between the Somali community and state and federal agencies, with immigration support, youth programs and benefits help. A peer example from another state.

entries.name: VOA Somali
entries.purpose: Somali-language daily radio programs, including morning, afternoon and evening editions. Items were dated October 30, 2026, when checked.

entries.name: BBC Somali
entries.purpose: Somali-language news service, founded in 1957, reaching the diaspora worldwide.

entries.name: Hiiraan Online
entries.purpose: News in Somali and English on Somalia, Somaliland, Puntland and the U.S. diaspora, with commentary, according to Stanford Libraries.

entries.name: Garowe Online
entries.purpose: Independent news site in English and Somali, a sister publication of Radio Garowe, according to Stanford Libraries.

entries.name: Universal TV
entries.purpose: Somali news and entertainment for the diaspora, with live streaming through its app. Somaliland authorities have obstructed it, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.

entries.name: SBS Somali
entries.purpose: Somali-language independent news and stories for listeners in Australia. The podcast can be reached from the United States.
